market_context: United States and Canada; mattress replacement decisions based on age, sagging, support, comfort, and condition.
title: How Often Should You Replace a Mattress?

seo.title: How Often to Replace a Mattress and How to Tell
seo.meta_description: Many mattresses are replaced around 6–8 years, but sagging, support loss, discomfort, and damage matter more than a fixed expiration date.
seo.search_intent: Determine how often a mattress should be replaced and recognize signs that replacement is actually needed.

excerpt: There is no universal expiration date for a mattress. Six to eight years is a useful general checkpoint, but replace sooner if there is permanent sagging, loss of support, recurring discomfort, or damage that maintenance cannot correct. A well-supported mattress that still performs well does not become unusable on a birthday.
content_html:
A mattress does not come with a warning light that switches on when its useful life is over. That is why “how often should I replace it?” is best answered with both a rough age range and a performance check.

Sleep Foundation uses about 6 to 8 years as a general replacement guideline. That is a checkpoint, not an expiration date. A badly sagging five-year-old mattress may need replacement sooner, while an older mattress that is still supportive and comfortable does not automatically fail because the calendar says eight.

Your body may notice the change before you do

If you regularly wake with stiffness or discomfort that improves when you sleep somewhere else, the mattress deserves a closer look. That does not prove the mattress is causing every ache, but a repeatable difference between beds is useful evidence.

Also notice whether you spend more time searching for a comfortable position, roll toward the same low spot, or feel as though you and a partner are being pulled toward the middle.

Permanent sagging matters more than surface wrinkles

A wrinkled cover or a temporary body impression is not necessarily a failure. The more meaningful sign is a depression that remains and changes how your body is supported.

Strip the bed and look across the mattress from the side. If one area is visibly lower, inspect the foundation too. A broken slat, bowed platform, or missing center support can make a good mattress look worn out.

Check what is underneath before buying what goes on top

Mattress manufacturers often specify maximum slat spacing, center supports, and acceptable foundations. A weak or incompatible base can shorten mattress life and may affect warranty coverage.

If the foundation is the problem, replacing only the mattress can put a new bed onto the same bad support and recreate the issue.

Construction type changes how wear appears

Foam, latex, innerspring, and hybrid mattresses do not age in exactly the same way. Even within one category, material quality varies enormously.

That makes hard rules such as “memory foam lasts exactly X years” less useful than they sound. Daily use, sleeper weight, heat, humidity, ventilation, and material density all influence how long support lasts.

Rotating can spread wear; it cannot rebuild support

Many modern mattresses can be rotated head-to-foot, while others have a one-sided construction and should not be flipped. Check the manufacturer's care instructions first.

Rotation can help distribute wear, particularly early in the mattress's life. It cannot repair a permanent sag, restore fatigued foam, or fix a damaged spring unit.

Condition can matter more than age

A washable protector, occasional vacuuming, and a dry, ventilated bedroom help keep a mattress clean. But cleaning the surface does not restore the internal structure.

If a mattress has been soaked by flooding, remained damp long enough for internal mold growth, or has contamination that cannot be safely cleaned and dried, replacement may make sense even when the mattress is relatively new.

A long warranty is not the same as a long comfort life

A 10- or 20-year warranty usually covers defined defects, not a promise that the mattress will feel identical for the entire period. Normal softening and comfort changes may not qualify.

If you suspect a defect, follow the warranty instructions for measuring sag and document the mattress, foundation, and purchase before disposing of anything.

So, should you replace yours now?

If the mattress is approaching 6–8 years, use that age as a reason to inspect it. If age is combined with permanent sagging, declining support, recurring sleep discomfort, structural noise, or visible damage, the case for replacement becomes much stronger.

If a newer mattress is clearly uncomfortable and you have ruled out the base and other obvious causes, you do not need to wait for an arbitrary anniversary.

The better question is not simply “how old is it?” but “is it still doing its job?” A mattress should support you consistently without asking your body to adapt to worn-out spots.

faq.question: Do I need to replace a mattress exactly every 8 years?
faq.answer: No. Six to eight years is a general checkpoint, not an expiration date. Condition, support, and sleep quality matter more than a precise age.

faq.question: Does sagging mean the mattress is worn out?
faq.answer: Permanent sag that changes support is a meaningful warning sign, but inspect the foundation or slats first to make sure the base is not causing it.

faq.question: Does rotating a mattress make it last longer?
faq.answer: Rotation can spread wear on models designed for it, but it cannot repair structural sagging. Follow the manufacturer's care instructions.

faq.question: Does a 10-year warranty mean the mattress should last 10 years?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Warranties cover defined defects; they do not guarantee unchanged comfort or support for the entire warranty period.
